## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Udapānadūsakajātaka* (Ja 271) is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka section of the Pali canon [Catalog]. Its framing verse opens with the words *Araññakassa isino* [Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related this story while residing at Isipatana, occasioned by a jackal that contaminated the monastic community's drinking-water well with excrement and urine [Fausböll 1879].

After novices pelted the jackal with clods of earth to drive it away, the monks discussed the incident in the Dhamma hall [Fausböll 1879]. The Buddha informed them that this was not the first time the jackal had defiled a well, recounting a past life set at Isipatana in Bārāṇasī [Fausböll 1879]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha revealed that the jackal of that time was the same jackal, while he himself had been the spiritual teacher (*gaṇasatthā*) [Fausböll 1879].
